Sixth grade science · Unit 2

Thermal Energy

Why does a metal spoon burn your fingers in hot soup while a wooden spoon doesn't? Why does a hot drink cool off by itself and never get hotter on the counter? Heat is energy on the move, carried by jiggling particles, and it follows rules you can predict.

Where we left off: in Unit 1, light that a surface absorbs does not vanish. You may already have learned that a black shirt gets hotter than a white one because it absorbs more light. This unit follows that absorbed energy and asks how heat moves, and why some materials pass it along faster than others.

heat flows this way

Put something hot next to something cold and thermal energy moves from the hot one to the cold one, never the other way around.

Concept 1 · What heat is

Temperature is average motion energy

Everything is made of tiny particles that never stop moving. Temperature tells you how much motion energy they have on average: hotter means faster jiggling. Thermal energy is the total of all that motion.

Analogy

A quiet library vs. a trampoline park

Both rooms hold the same number of kids. In the library, kids shuffle slowly; in the trampoline park, they bounce and sprint. Temperature is the average motion energy of the kids.

Thermal energy is the total energy of all of them. Add more kids to the trampoline park and the total goes up even if nobody bounces any faster. That is why a bathtub of warm water can hold more thermal energy than a red-hot nail.

Try it

Turn up the heat

Predict. Will the particles move faster, slower, or the same when the temperature goes up? Will they all move at exactly the same speed?

Do. Start at 20 °C (room temperature). Drag the slider to 0, then to 100, and watch the box and the speed readout at each stop.

Notice. At 100 °C the particles race around and bump hard, and they turn redder. At 0 °C they barely move. At any one setting they still do not all move at the same speed: the temperature tells you the average.

Why it matters. Temperature is not a thing that flows. It is a measure of how fast the particles are moving, on average. That is why heating something makes it expand, melt, or boil.

Data

Same temperature, very different thermal energy

A cup and a bathtub of water are both 40 °C. The particles move equally fast, but a bathtub has far more particles, so far more total thermal energy.

Thermal energy ≈ mass × 4.18 J per gram per °C × temperature rise above 0 °C. Rounded values.

Concept 2 · How heat travels

Three paths for heat

Heat moves three ways: conduction (touching), convection (moving fluid), and radiation (light, no touching needed).

Diagram

Bump, flow, glow: three paths for heat

Conduction: bumping along

Hot particles shake hard and bump their neighbors, who bump the next ones, like a bucket brigade. Nobody travels; only the energy does. That is how the handle of a spoon warms up in soup.

Convection: a loop of moving fluid

In a liquid or gas, warm fluid rises and cool fluid sinks, so the whole fluid rides a loop that carries energy. This only works in a fluid that can flow.

Radiation: light carries the energy

Warmth on your hands across empty air. Light carries the energy, so no touching and no moving fluid are needed. It is how the Sun's energy crosses empty space to Earth.

Data

How fast do materials pass heat along?

Copper passes heat along more than 10,000 times faster than air does.

Thermal conductivity in watts per meter per degree Celsius (W/m·K), rounded, at room temperature. A bigger number means heat conducts faster. The bars use a log scale, so a small difference in bar length is a big difference in the number.

Data

The three paths at a glance

PathNeeds matter?A number to rememberEveryday example
ConductionYes, touchingCopper about 400 vs. air about 0.03 W/m·KMetal spoon in hot soup
ConvectionYes, a fluid that can flowWarmer fluid is less dense, so it risesWarm air near a radiator, boiling pot
RadiationNoSunlight: about 1,360 watts on each square meter above the atmosphere; takes about 8 minutes to reach usSun on your face, campfire glow
Go deeper: what is really happening in each path

Conduction. In metals, loose electrons carry energy quickly, so metals are the best conductors. In wood and plastic, energy has to hop from one jiggling particle to the next, which is slow. Gases such as air are poor conductors because their particles are far apart and rarely bump.

Convection. Warm fluid expands, so it is less dense than the cooler fluid around it and gets pushed upward. Gravity does the pushing. Weather, ocean currents, and the warm air over a heater are all examples of convection. A fan or a spoon stirring soup makes convection faster.

Radiation. Every object gives off infrared light, and hotter objects give off more. Dark, rough surfaces absorb and give off radiation better than shiny ones. Radiation needs no matter to carry it, which is why it can cross empty space.

Try it

Heat the pot and watch the loop

Diagram

Why does warm stuff rise?

When particles speed up they take up more room. The same box holds fewer of them, so warm fluid is lighter and floats up, like a hot-air balloon.

Concept 3 · Conductors and insulators

Why metal feels cold

Some materials pass heat fast (conductors) and some pass it slowly (insulators). Metal feels cold because it pulls heat out of your hand quickly.

Analogy

A fast lane vs. a rocky trail

Heat moves through metal like traffic on a wide-open highway. In wood, plastic, and air, it crawls along a rocky trail. Both a metal spoon and a wooden spoon in the same room are the same temperature. The metal one feels colder because it drains heat from your hand fast; the wood one barely takes any, so your hand stays warm. (Metals have loose electrons that carry energy; in wood and plastic, energy has to hop slowly from particle to particle.)

Where it breaks: the highway does not keep the cars. The heat spreads along the spoon and into the air; metal just moves it quickly.

Diagram

How a thermos works

A thermos blocks all three paths, so your soup stays hot and your lemonade stays cold.

PartWhat it blocks
Vacuum gap between two wallsConduction and convection: with almost no particles in the gap, there is nothing to bump or to flow
Shiny (silvered) wallsRadiation: they reflect heat rays back toward the drink
Stopper or lidConvection and evaporation out the top; plastic also slows conduction
Plastic or steel outer shellProtects the thin inner walls and keeps your hand from feeling the heat

The gap is a vacuum: most of the air has been pumped out. Radiation does not need particles, so the shiny coating is the second line of defense. A thermos does not stop heat completely. A little still leaks out through the stopper and the rim where the two walls join, so the drink slowly cools. The vacuum flask was invented by the Scottish scientist James Dewar in 1892.

Try it in your head: a cold drink in a thermos stays cold for the same reason. The three heat paths are blocked in the other direction, so heat from the warm room cannot get in.

Build it

Engineering challenge: the ice keeper

The problem: keep 3 ice cubes from melting for 30 minutes. Heat always flows from the warm room into the cold ice, so your job is to slow down every path it can take.

Criteria: less meltwater than a bare cup of ice sitting right next to yours. Least meltwater wins.

Constraints: 1 cup, 2 sheets of paper, 30 cm of foil, 5 cotton balls, 1 sandwich bag, and 1 meter of tape. No freezer, no ice packs.

  1. Try it in the game first. Play Thermos Defense at the bottom of this page. Notice that each blocker stops only one heat path.
  2. Plan. Sketch two different ideas on your design log. Label which path each part blocks: conduction, convection, or radiation.
  3. Build and test. Start your cup and the bare cup at the same time, on the same table, away from sunny windows. After 30 minutes, pour off the meltwater and measure it in mL.
  4. Improve. Change one thing, test again, and record it.

Print a design log for each team. The bare cup is your control: same ice, same room, same time, so the only difference is your design (Unit 0).

Concept 4 · Which way does heat go?

Always hot to cold

Heat always flows from hot to cold until both are the same temperature. That is called thermal equilibrium.

Analogy

Two tanks joined by a pipe

Water only flows downhill, and heat only flows "downhill" in temperature. When the levels match, the flow stops: that's equilibrium.

Try it

Mix hot water and cold water

Data

A hot drink cools toward room temperature

The drink never drops below room temperature on its own: once the levels match, the flow stops. Teaching model with typical time constants.

Concept 5 · Heating and changing state

Why ice stays at 0 °C (32 °F) while it melts

While a substance melts or boils, the energy you add goes into loosening the bonds between particles, not into speeding them up. So the temperature stops rising.

Analogy

Climbing stairs with long landings

Imagine climbing a building's stairs with long flat landings. On the steps, every stride lifts you higher: that is temperature rising. On a landing you keep walking, so you keep spending energy, but your height does not change. That is melting or boiling: the energy you add goes into loosening the grip between particles, not into speeding them up, so the thermometer stays put. When the grip is broken, you reach the next set of steps and the temperature climbs again.

Where it breaks: on a real landing you choose to walk. In water the flat part is forced, and the boiling landing is far longer than the melting one: boiling takes about 7 times as much energy per gram (the picture is not to scale).

Try it

Add energy to 1 g of ice

Predict. You start with 1 g of ice at -20 °C and add energy a little at a time. Predict: does the temperature rise the whole way? When might it stop rising?

Do. Slide the energy from 0 up to about 3,100 J in small steps. Pause often and read the temperature, the stage name, and the dot on the graph. Look at 0 to 100 J, then 100 to 400 J, then 400 to 800 J.

Notice. Between about 42 J and 376 J the temperature sits at 0 °C even though you keep adding energy, and the picture changes from a tight lattice to loose particles. It does the same thing at 100 °C between about 794 J and 3,054 J. Melting needs roughly 334 J per gram; boiling needs roughly 2,260 J per gram.

Why it matters. During melting and boiling, the energy goes into loosening the grip particles have on each other, not into speeding them up. That is why a pot of boiling water stays at 100 °C no matter how high you turn the burner, and why ice water stays cold until the last ice is gone.

Data

The heating curve of water

Using rounded values: ice 2.1 J per gram per °C, melting 334 J per gram, liquid 4.18 J per gram per °C, boiling 2,260 J per gram, steam 2.0 J per gram per °C. Boiling takes almost seven times as much energy as melting. Compare it with the staircase above: each flat landing is a flat step on this curve.

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

Why does the metal spoon burn your fingers while the wooden spoon doesn't, and why does the soup eventually cool?

Show a model answer

Spoon: metal is a conductor, so heat travels quickly from the soup along the spoon into your fingers. Wood is an insulator, so the heat crawls.

Cooling: heat always flows from hot to cold. The soup is hotter than the air and bowl, so it loses thermal energy until it reaches room temperature.

Words to know

thermal energy
Total motion energy of all the particles in an object.
temperature
Average motion energy of the particles.
heat
Thermal energy moving from a hotter place to a colder one.
conduction
Heat passed by particles bumping each other.
convection
Heat carried by moving liquid or gas.
radiation
Heat carried by light waves, no matter needed.
conductor
Material that passes heat quickly.
insulator
Material that passes heat slowly.
equilibrium
When two things reach the same temperature and heat stops flowing.
state of matter
Solid, liquid, or gas.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $10): two thermometers, three or four cups, hot and cold tap water, metal/plastic/wooden spoons, butter and toothpicks, food coloring, ice cubes, a foam cup and a lid, aluminum foil. For the ice keeper: cotton balls, sandwich bags, tape, and a measuring cup marked in mL.

  • Concept 1: compare a cup and a pot of equally warm water. Which holds heat longer?
  • Concept 2: drop a bit of food coloring in warm water and in cold water. Watch the warm plume rise (convection). Hold hands near a lamp (radiation).
  • Concept 3: dab butter on three spoons, stand them in hot water, and see which beads fall off first. Then run the ice keeper challenge (about 60 minutes including the 30-minute test).
  • Concept 4: mix hot and cold water and check the thermometer against the prediction.
  • Concept 5: stir ice water with a thermometer while the ice melts and note that it stays at 0 °C.

Common misconceptions:

  • "Cold flows into your hand." Heat flows out of the hand. There is no cold substance.
  • "Metal is colder than wood." They're the same temperature. Metal just removes heat faster.
  • "Heat rises." Hot fluid rises. Conduction goes in every direction.
  • "Temperature and heat are the same." Temperature is average motion energy per particle; thermal energy depends on how much material you have.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions, one per concept.

After the lesson · Game

Play: Thermos Defense

Keep a mug of cocoa hot. Heat leaks out by conduction, convection and radiation, and in this game each blocker only stops one of them. Pick the right ones before the clock runs.
